Consideration of the motion of Mr. Kelly for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr.. Sutherland, resumed from Friday, March 7.
Mr. HANCE J. LOGAN (Cumberland): Mr. Speaker, joining with others I desire to congratulate the mover (Mr. Kelly), and the seconder (Mr. Lapierre) of the Address. We have known the member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) for a long time; we know how eloquent he is. I hail in this House a fellow Nova Scotian in the member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Kelly), who in

moving the Address gave us one of the most businesslike speeches we have listened to for some sessions. I am going to speak to-day in perhaps a rather candid way. I agree with my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St George (Mr. Marler) who told us on Thursday that speeches in this debate should be rather in the direction of advice to the government of the country, and should reflect the views of the constituencies which the speakers represent.	I propose this afternoon, in a
most humble way, to give some advice to the government of Canada particularly in reference to the Maritime provinces to which I have the honour to belong.
The Speech from the Throne itself, as a whole, is one which commends itself to all well-wishers of Canada. If previously we had a chart we now have a definite programme to deal with at this session. Speaking as a Liberal I regard the Speech from the Throne as one calculated to give us fresh hope for the welfare of this country. Undoubtedly the speech is long, consisting as it does of twenty-one or twenty-two paragraphs, but every paragraph is important in view of the present condition of affairs with which we have to cope. I shall refer particularly, Mr. Speaker, to one or two of these paragraphs in passing. Paragraph 4 is thus worded:
My ministers believe, however, that in virtue of economies already effected they will, when the present financial year closes, be able to announce to the country that for the first time since 1912-1913 the national budget has been balanced. They are further of the opinion that when the budget for the ensuing fiscal year is introduced it will be found that the relation between public revenue and public expenditure is such as to justify some immediate reduction of taxation.
The people of this country will welcome this declaration of an early reduction in taxation with a great deal of pleasure. We know that the war was expensive. We were quite willing during that great struggle to bear our burden. But the taxation of this country at the present time-I refer particularly to the direct taxation-is, in my humble judgment, too high, and is not in the best interests of the country as a whole.
In the next paragraph the government announce that the government propose
-to reduce the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, thereby aiding materially in the development of our natural resources, and, through cheapened production, effecting a diminution also in the cost of living.
That is a good sound Liberal principle, a doctrine which we desire to preach and to carry out. The wealth of Canada can never be built up with exotic industries. The great

The Address-Mr. Logan
wealth of Canada depends upon the soil, upon the sea, upon the forest, upon the mines, and whatever we can do to lessen the cost of production in connection with these great natural resources, the richer our country must become. This doctrine is particularly pleasing to one from Nova Scotia, because there we not only have the important industry of agriculture but we also have the great mining industry, we have the lumbering industry, and we have the great fishing industry. A reduction in the cost of production will be beneficial to these industries as well as to agriculture. One would think sometimes when an industry affecting a few hundred men is getting nervous, that there were not other large industries in Canada which should be considered. I read an address the other day delivered by my hon. friend the member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) before an organization in this city in which he made this statement:
One hundred thousand of the inhabitants of Canada are dependent upon the fishing industry.
What in the name of heaven has protection ever done for the fishing industry of this country? We have in Nova Scotia probably nearly one hundred thousand people directly or indirectly dependent upon the coal mining industry. What has protection ever done for the coal mining industry of this Dominion? I will devote some little time later on in my address to a consideration of the question of the duty upon coal. I want to remove from the minds of the people of Canada the idea that we have any protection upon the production of coal. Then, too, what has protection ever done for the lumbering industry of the Maritime provinces, or for that matter what has it ever done for the agricultural interests of these provinces? Forty-five years have gone by since great hopes were held out to us. We were promised in that distant past that the National Policy would build up great industries in the Maritime provinces, that smokestacks would arise in all parts of the country, and that incidentally there would be a great market for the products of the farm. We have waited for forty-five years for this prediction to be fulfilled. I defy anybody in this House, from the leader of the opposition down, to show where high protection has been of benefit to the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Why, Sir, the two industries in my constituency that have really weathered the storm, so to speak- have weathered the hard times that followed the war-are the woollen industry in Oxford and the boot and shoe industry in Amherst. They were prosperous industries away back
in the seventies before we had any National Policy; but some other industries particularly those which have been built up on a false basis were the ones to suffer first when depression came a few years ago.
Mr. Speaker, we have had it stated here there is prosperity in Canada. The leader of the opposition denies it, but I prefer to take the language of a man who occupies a very important position, namely R. S. White, editor in chief of the Montreal Gazette, the sanest Conservative newspaper in Canada. In his opening remarks in the book published this year by the Gazette company containing a commercial and financial review of the year 1923 he says:
Surveying the state of trade in Canada in 1923, and all that pertains to the material prosperity of its people, there is much to encourage and little to dispirit.
Taking the whole of the Dominion of Canada "there is much to encourage and little to dispirit," but we must admit there are districts in Canada which have not the prosperity which we would wish. Those districts are the prairie provinces of the West and the Maritime provinces. We on this side desire to endeavour to better conditions in these two parts of Canada, believing as we do that the strength of our confederation chain depends upon the strength of the individual links. It is of no use to try to build up a strong Canada when the Maritime provinces are weak or are not prospering. The Maritime provinces were considered most important to confederation, and they are most important. But if the conditions there are ijot what they should be, it behooves this government, or any other government in this country, to get down, as my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) often says, to brass tacks, to find out what is the matter, and effect a remedy, if possible.
Referring again to the general prosperity of Canada outside of these two parts thereof, it is a matter of congratulation that there has been and is considerable prosperity. I know it is stated that we are very heavily in debt, that we owe about two billions four hundred millions of money, but does it ever occur to you, Mr. Speaker, that three-quarters of that money is due to Canadians, and that the people of Canada actually receive every year from that loan about ninety million dollars in interest? The government pays in pensions to the soldiers thirty-three million dollars. That money is kept in Canada; it circulates again, and part of it comes back to the treasury of the country. We advanced to railways something like seventy-seven millions last year, but was that money sent out of the country? No, it was paid
The Address-Mr. Logan

out to working men, to manufacturers, and producers throughout the length and breadth of the land. We gave subsidies to the provinces of twelve million dollars which is spent in the provinces and is coming back to us in an indirect way. We gave in grants for secular education, for highways and agriculture, eight million dollars, and in ordinary expenditure about one hundred and twenty-six million dollars, all spent in Canada, and paid to Canadians. Our total expenditure for the year was about four hundred and thirty-four million. I venture to state that out of that sum three hundred and seventy-five million dollars remained in Canada, that being one of the reasons why this country is as prosperous as it is to-day. If hon. members will look at the deposits in the savings banks and in the chartered banks of the country, they will find that in spite of the fact that the Canadians have one billion seven hundred millions invested in government bonds, the deposits in the chartered banks and in the savings banks have materially increased during the last year. Therefore, I think it can be very well said that, so far as the central part of Canada is concerned there is prosperity and considerable of it.
What is the matter, may I ask, with the Maritime provinces? I am not going to speak of the prairie provinces, because there are so many honourable gentlemen from those provinces who know so much more about them than I do that it would be presumptuous on my part to speak about their difficulties. But I .do claim to know something about the difficulties of the Maritime provinces. What are the difficulties? What is the cause of this depression? Why is it that so many of our manufactories are idle? Why is it that the grass grows upon the streets of many of the seaport towns of those provinces? I give you the answer, Mr. Speaker, in two words. Tariff and transportation are the causes of it. We did not feel the effects of the National Policy as long as we had cheap transportation. We did not feel it so severely as we feel it now, so long as we could transport our manufactured goods from the Maritime provinces into the middle of Canada or the West at a low rate of freight. But, a few years ago, when the late government merged the Intercolonial with the commercial railways of Canada, and raised the freight rates to their present position, we found ourselves not only up against a tariff wall, but up against a freight wall, and between the two walls we are being squeezed to death.

Let us stress for a moment what happened in the Maritime provinces. Hon. members will pardon me if I go over this matter, not at as great length as I have on other occasions in the House, but to some extent to follow up my arguments. In the Maritime provinces, let it be understood and known, before confederation we were a comparatively rich people. The trade per capita of New Brunswick, let me tell hon. members, in 1864 was almost double that of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, known as old Canada, and the trade of Nova Scotia was materially greater than the trade of Canada. We owned at that time in Nova Scotia over three thousand ships which sailed out of our ports carrying products of the farms, forests, mines and fisheries. Where did they carry that produce? They earned it especially to the New England states and to the West Indies. We had at that time seventeen thousand of our sons upon the sea, manning ships, sailing through the different waters, particularly those which I have mentioned. We did not desire confederation. Let that also be distinctly understood; and so great an optimist as my very distinguished predecessor in the representation of Cumberland, that great Canadian, Sir Charles Tupper, Baronet, in 1864, three years before confederation, made the statement in the House of Assembly in Nova Scotia that the difficulties of confederation were insuperable. Shortly after that our men met in Charlottetown to form a Maritime union. While there a delegation from Upper and Lower Canada, the greatest galaxy of orators probably that ever sailed the Maritime seas-Sir John Macdonald, Hon. George Brown, D'Arcy McGee, Sir Hector Langevin, and many others of the great political stars of the country-came in upon our little convention, and said, "Walk into our parlor of confederation." The representatives of the Maritime provinces said, "No, there are too great difficulties." They said, "What are they? What are you afraid of." Our representatives said, "We are afraid, first that you will raise a tariff in this country that will by a retaliatory tariff interfere with our trade with that country which nature intended we should trade with, namely the New England states of America. If we are shut out from that market, where are we? Where is our market to come from?" With honeyed words, these orators said, "We will give you a new market to take the place of this market if you should lose it." Our delegates said to them, "How can you give us that market? You are too far away." They replied, "We will build you a means of communication, namely the Intercolonial, in order that if you

The Address-Mr. Logan
lose the United States market you will have a market equally as good in the central parts of Canada." Our people listened to them. They did not however take their word; they insisted it should be in the bond, and if hon. members will read section 145 of the British North America Act they will find set out in that section not only the promised building of the Intercolonial, but the reasons why it would be built, namely to secure the consent of the people of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to enter confederation. For fifty years the promises given at the time of confederation were fairly well kept. As I say, we did not feel the effect of the National Policy or high protection in this country as long as we were able to send our goods from the Maritime provinces to the West. We used to boast in the young city in which I live that we sent over half of our products to western Canada. We send mighty little of our production to western Canada or to central Canada today, because we are shut out of those markets by the exorbitant rates that have been put into effect upon the railways of our country, the Intercolonial included.
It is difficult for us to make the people of the rest of Canada understand our grievance in this matter, and it is difficult for them to know just how sensitive we are. There are many still living that remember the fight for confederation. It is still an unpopular subject to discuss. They know, and we, their sons, know that those solemn promises were made and we know that when the Intercolonial railway ceased to be a part of the constitution of this country and was placed among commercial railways of Canada and under the same rates of freight, a crime was committed against the people of the Maritime provinces. We are here to-day again to ask and demand that those promises made to us in 1864, 1865 and 1866, promises which I could repeat here for an hour if I cared to weary you, must be kept if we are to be at all prosperous and to become the part of confederation that we should be.
Before leaving this subject, let me say that we in the Maritime provinces feel grateful for some things that have been done by this government. Under the old government, our whole road was controlled in Toronto by [DOT] Canadian Northern officials, men who had no sympathy with us and with whom we did not have much acquaintance. This government has changed that. We have had established at Moncton headquarters for the government railways in the Maritime provinces. They are in charge of a Maritime province man. The general superintendent is
a Maritime province man, and equally pleasant is the fact that the general traffic manager is also a Maritime province man. We have, as I say, many things to be thankful for to this government for ameliorating the conditions that existed there four or five years ago. But I want to say now to the government and to the country that until conditions are made better as regards freight rates in the Maritime provinces, not from an economic standpoint altogether, but from a constitutional standpoint, we never can be satisfied in those provinces, and the government is bound to find that out. They found it out in the constituency of Halifax. They found it out in the constituency of Kent. Nobody in Halifax spoke about protection; even the hon. member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter) did not talk protection in Halifax. He did not talk protection in Kent. Why? That would be ridiculous; nobody wanted to hear about protection. But what he did talk about was the grievances of the Maritime provinces, and the people feel those grievances and they must be remedied.
Did I understand the hon. member to say that those appointments to executive positions on the railways were made by the government?

Indirectly by the government. They were made by Sir Henry Thornton and his board, and Sir Henry Thornton and his board were appointed by the government, so indirectly they were appointed by the government.
Having stated the reason for the depression in the Maritime provinces, let me suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this House, some things that may bring back our prosperity. In the first place, we desire export trade. We are, it has been well said, the eastern wharf of Canada. But our export trade has diminished and does not bring to us that prosperity which we formerly enjoyed. Our natural market, besides that of the United States, is to the south of us. We looked, in days gone by, to the United States. That market is closed to us by the Fordney tariff. We then looked to central and western Canada for trade. That market is closed to us by the freight tariff. Where are we to look now? We are to look to the place where we always should have looked, namely, across water transportation to the countries to the south of us. Export trade with the West Indies and with South America should be encouraged in every possible way. Trade with those countries should be built up and looked after. During this winter I

ly as good as the American anthracite. So the old argument against bituminous coal, the old horror that the people had against the smoke, has passed away, and now we have a substitute for anthracite which is equally as good as anthracite.
We imported into this country -last year- and these figures are well within the mark-coal to the value of over $100,000,000. Of that about 14,000,000 tons was bituminous coal and 5,000,000 tons anthracite. In converting bituminous coal into coke, one-and-a-half tons of coal are required to make one ton of coke; so if we had desired last year to replace the five million tons of anthracite brought into this country with coke, it would have meant the mining of an additional
7.500,000	tons of bituminous coal in this country. Therefore if we had a policy by which this country could be made self-contained so far as coal is concerned, we would not only prevent the importation of 14.000,000 tons of bituminous coal each year, but by making coke to take the place of anthracite, we would add 7,500,000 tons more to that
14,000,000 tons, making a total of 21,500.000 tons of extra coal mined in this country to replace the American coal now imported. We are producing about 18,000.000 tons, >but if we had a proper coal policy we would add I repeat no less a quantity than 21,500,000 tons of coal mined in this country, which, at a price of $5 a ton at the mines would mean to the miners and operators and all those connected with the collieries, no less a sum than $107,500,000. In addition to that, we would have transportation costs paid to the Canadian National Railways, at say $4 per ton, amounting to $86,000,000, which would also be left in Canada to help the people of this country. Further, let me point this out. When we buy $100,000,000 of coal in the United States we have to pay in exchange, according to the rate that is being charged to-day, no less a sum than $3,500,000 of good Canadian money. That money goes in exchange, and might just as well be thrown into the sea. If you add the saving in exchange to the extra amount which would be spent in Canada for producing the coal and add to that again the cost of transportation which would be paid to Canadian railways, you get a total amount of good Canadian money which would be left here of nearly $200,000,000.
New, let me just refer again to discount on exchange. We pay it largely because we are buying so much from the United States of America. If we could reduce the amount we
fMr. Logan.]
are paying to the United States by that $100,000,000 which we paid for coal imported last year, in all probability we would have had par money in this country at the present time, because that would have helped to bring the imports and exports as between the two countries almost to the same level. If we did that we would save the exchange upon the whole purchase price of articles other than coal brought into this country from the United States, amounting to about $520,000,000. A rate of three and a half per cent on $520,000,000 would represent over $18,000,000 more saved to the country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, how is coal independence to be secured? One way of bringing about that most desirable result is to provide transportation for our coal at a reasonable rate. Last year the Mines committee of the House dealt with this matter. We listened to a great amount of very valuable information from different persons in reference to coal and the transportation thereof. We had before us transportation men, we had freight agents, we had traffic managers, we had all kinds of officials to advise us as to how we could handle coal. We also had before us some men who were not connected with any transportation company. For example, there was Mr. M. J. Butler, formerly deputy minister of railways in this country, who afterwards became general manager of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, and subsequently was connected with the Armstrong-Whitworth Company, one of the largest concerns in the British Empire, a man of outstanding ability. He put before us arguments which I will not go into but will condense in this way: He said that instead of it costing us $9 or $12, which is the price to-day I believe, for transporting coal, from Edmonton or even west of that city to Toronto, coal could be put in Toronto for $4.57 a ton; that was he contended the actual cost of it. Mr. Butler was not a man picked off the street but a gentleman of knowledge and of standing in the country, and he put this statement in concise form before us. He, of course, made a condition that I submit is the crux of the whole matter, that if we are going to transport coal cheaply it must be done with proper equipment; it is no use trying to transport coal in broken-down equipment. Let me use his own language on that point:
To begin with let us eliminate the "know it can't be done type." Let us also eliminate the traffic officers who are making rates, predicated before using, small coal cars, box cars, old weak locomotives, with small train loads- or mixed train loads, with a few cars of coal to fdl up the tonnage.

The Address-Mr. Logan
It is I think clear, that the problem is one that demands that the equipment, from beginning to end shall be adequate to handle the tonnage at the lowest cost, but not at a price that the railway will suffer.
The argument that Mr. Butler makes is that we must provide the equipment in order to carry coal, and if we do that there will be a very material lessening in the cost. Therefore I submit to the government they should immediately appoint a commission, to consist of not more than three men, to make a report to the House as to the actual facts in reference to the cost of transporting coal. I am not talking about the question of income, of net revenue or gross revenue; I want to know what it actually costs to transport coal in Canada. It is almost impossible to get that knowledge from a railway official. One man may be charging $5 and it is difficult for him, perhaps, to explain the discrepancy if the cost is only $3. T1 en we must remember there is always a certain amount of hesitancy on the part of officials of competing companies to disclose information which might affect either corporation. What we want to do is to get down to the actual cost of carrying coal. Mr. Butler informed us that the Virginia railway is carrying coal at a very low rate, and upon that rate he has founded the rates which could be made by the railways of Canada. I therefore submit that a commission should be appointed to inquire into this matter. I would suggest that Mr. Butler be made chairman of the commission, and that a man from Alberta and a man from the Maritime provinces should be associated with him. This commission should be given power to go down into the territory of the Virginia railway where these rates exist-and, mark you, the grades there are higher than we have; do not forget that, the grades in Virginia add nothing to their advantage that I can seethe commission should also investigate the transportation costs of the Norfolk and Western, and the Chesapeake and Ohio, and the Illinois Central. In this way, I believe, it can be established what is the actual cost of carrying coal. I believe myself that if this inquiry be made it will establish that coal can be carried, from the Maritime provinces for instance to the province of Ontario, for not more-than $2 a ton at the very outside. We used to pay $1.60 six or seven years ago from the Cumberland mines, Nova Scotia, to Montreal. The present rate is $3.60 or $3.80. I want to know what the actual cost of carrying that coal is, I do not want it from any railway official, I want it from a man who is independent of all transportation companies and not concerned in the importation of 12
American coal. I believe we can do that by carrying out my suggestion; I believe we can get down to the very basis of the matter, get down to rock bottom, and find out what the transportation of coal costs. We shall then know what percentage ought to be allowed to our railwaj's in order to enable them to make a profit.
I am now going to refer to another matter which I think is important to the Maritime provinces, and indeed to all Canada. In the Speech from the Throne it is mentioned that it is proposed to make every effort to develop still further the policy of Canadian trade via Canadian ports. Last year the Minister of Finance brought down a measure giving ten per cent reduction on British goods when imported through Canadian ports. I shall not now discuss whether that policy was right or wrong. There is a strong argument being made by the woollen people of this country that owing to the present depreciation of English currency, the unemployment situation in the United Kingdom, and the lower labour rates- as a result in a word of the operation of the law of supply and demand-that we, perhaps, made a mistake at that time in lessening the duty on woollen goods entering Canada. I am not now going to discuss the pros and cons of that question. What I want to argue is that the government should go the whole way and confine the British preference to goods brought in through Canadian ocean or river ports. I may say, however, that even with the ten per cent reduction in duty a marvellous diversion of shipments has been made to Canadian ports since the last budget. I have not the figures relating to this matter at the present time, but I presume they will be presented to us when the budget is brought down. I cannot see myself, any reason why we should not follow the historic policy of the United States and confine this preference entirely to goods brought in through our sea and river ports.
In the Speech from the Throne a reference is made to the Imperial Conference and the Imperial Economic Conference held in London last year. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speakers'who have so far taken part in this debate. I believe they all think as I do, that this is a serious time in the history of our country. Perhaps it would not be out of place to paraphrase in this connection, the motto which is given to students when striving to acquire a knowledge of typewriting: "Now is the time for all good men to come to the aid of the country." This is a good time for us to consider these matters seriously, because it is a serious time in the history of our land.

The Address-Mr. Logan

But I do resent one statement and that was the attack that was made during this debate on the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Mackenzie King), for not taking part, in the recent general elections in Great Britain on behalf of Mr. Baldwin's preferential tariff. I want to point out that, in my humble opinion, such interference in the British elections would have been resented just as strongly as would interference by the British prime minister in an election campaign in Canada. What are the facts? The Imperial Conference was called by the Baldwin government. The Dominions responded to the call and journeyed to London. After many weeks of conference it was agreed by the government of Great Britain to extend the preference on certain products of the Dominion. This was promised from the Old Land to sister nations in this great British commonwealth, and I insist that these promises are binding upon the homeland. Are we to be told that the British parliament which, a few years ago, although the great majority thereof was hostile to home rule, carried out an undertaking of its predecessors, and thus kept faith with southern Ireland, is going to break faith with Canada and the other sister nations? I refuse to believe it. The Baldwin government entered into a certain agreement with the United States before they went out of power, extending the right of seizure beyond the three-mile limit. Will anyone suggest that the Ramsay MacDonald government is not going to carry out to the letter its agreement with its predecessors in office. Surely we are to be treated as well, at least, as foreign nations. If not, then our faith in future imperial conferences is going to be materially lessened. So far from the Prime Minister of the country being criticized for not taking part in that election, I am sure he should be praised for the silence he maintained.
I want to advocate before I take my seat that the railway department of this country -and I now direct my remarks principally to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), to Sir Henry Thornton and his board-should endeavour to carry more produce and more exports to Canadian ports. I desire to make an argument, Mr. Speaker, upon this line, following the statutes that have been passed in this country. I think we sometimes forget about them. Let us go back to 1903 and refer to page 455 of the statutes of that year, being 3 Edward VTI, Chap. 71, an Act respecting the Construction of a Canadian National Transcontinental Railway. It ratified and confirmed the agreement between His Majesty and the Grand Trunk Pacific

Railway Company, which agreement forms the schedule to the act. The agreement recites among other things-and bear these words in mind-that the object is-
To secure the most direct and economical interchange of traffic between eastern Canada and the provinces west of the great lakes, to open up and develop the northern zone of the Dominion, to promote the internal and foreign trade of Canada, and to develop commerce through Canadian ports.
Section 42 reads:
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of the railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory, or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports.
Section 43 reads:
The company further agrees that it shall not, in any matter within its power, directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those above provided, but shall, in all respects, in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely-the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports.
Section 45 provides:

I grow cattle as well as wheat, and my cattle are grown on an export basis the same as wheat. How are you going to protect me on the cattle?

I have been diverted from my subject and as I want to finish by six o'clock I will hurry on. I say this, Mr. Speaker, to my hon. friends in particular. They have more to gain from the cheapening of transportation than from the removal of any tariff. I would exhaust the resources of this country in cheapening transportation from western Canada to the seaboard. I would do it in two or three different ways. I would, as I did last year, vote for any appropriation that is necessary to develop to its ultimate limits the port of Vancouver. If it is possible to take the grain of any of the western provinces out by Vancouver at a lower rate, I am in favour of that. Last session I went so far as to vote for the Hudson Bay railway, although I do not believe for a minute that it is ever going to give lower rates or any relief for the western farmer. Yet, it may open up a country that has some other resources, and it may pay for itself in that way. But I cannot believe the wheat will ever go out by that route. The great thing is the development of the St. Lawrence river so that ocean vessels will go up to the head of the lakes as they did last year, and take cargoes of wheat right over to Liverpool. I do not think that is the inevitable or the natural development of that route; but if the St. Lawrence river were improved to give a twenty-five or thirty-foot draft, big ships that take 500,000 bushels of grain would load at Fort William and would probably break bulk at the city of Quebec. It might be the city of Three Rivers.
It is the better place.

But Montreal and Quebec should, under those conditions, develop into two of the greatest ports on the North American continent.

The Address-Mr. Hocken
An lion. MEMBER: What about Toronto?

Toronto gets nothing out of this. A ship may come in with package freight, but there are no bulk cargoes to receive from or to deliver in Toronto. A vessel holding 500,000 bushels of wheat would leave Fort William, go down to the city of Quebec and discharge into ocean boats which would go across to Liverpool, or to any other port in the world, in that way saving five to eight cents a bushel on wheat. If from five to eight cents a bushel could be saved on the wheat that was grown on the western prairies last year, the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) can figure out what that means. That is one of the ways in which transportation can be cheapened. Water transportation, as we all know, can be done at much lower rates than rail transporation.
I have another plan to suggest, and I am now going, to venture into the realm of prophecy. Having had the example a day or so ago of the dean of the House, the hon. member for South York ( Mr. Maclean), who is something of a prophet, I am going to make a suggestion that may seem a little in advance of the time, but which, I will venture to predict, before many years will be a subject of serious discussion as a progressive policy for this country. I think the real reduction in the cost of transportation is to come from the electrification of the railways. I believe there are men sitting in this House to-day, yes, men in middle life or past it, who will live to see our whole western railway system electrified. If that is done, the railways will be run with at least 50 per cent greater efficiency than they have to-day. The efficiency of a railway train lies in the locomotive. An electric locomotive, by actual experience, on the New York, New Haven and Hartford line, showed an increased efficiency over steam of fifty to sixty per cent. Electric locomotives take longer trains; they take heavier grades; they eliminate all the water service and they are more efficient in every particular. Every 100 or 150 miles a steam locomotive operates, it goes into the shops to be repaired. On the New York, New Haven and Hartford railway, they inspect an electric locomotive every 1,800 miles it runs. I have some figures here that are, perhaps, worth while mentioning.
One of these statements is that in the United States to-day they are operating 5,000 miles of regular railroad on which trains are hauled by electric locomotives. On those railroads ordinary passenger and freight trains made up into ordinary trains are hauled by electricity. That is a very considerable mileage. On the Milwaukee line, they have found an increase in efficiency of 50 per cent. On some lines, they have done better. Mr. Ralston, of the New York, New Haven and Hartford line, says that there has been only one failure of a locomotive in every 21,000 miles run by electricity, whereas there is one failure for every 4,000 miles run under steam. Thirty-three electric locomotives have handled the passenger traffic in and out of the Pennsylvania terminals of New York for eleven years. They have made more than 7,000,000 miles with a record of 64 4-37 miles per detention on account of the locomotives. They have made 11,454 miles for every minute of detention. The maintenance of these locomotives over all this long time has been just about one-sixth of equivalent steam locomotives.
My suggestion-and I think it will come to pass-is that there should be constructed in every province in the West a great power plant for the purpose of operating those railways, and at the same time of supplying power to every municipality in the province. There should be. a super-power zone such as they are talking about in the Atlantic states of the union. It is already proposed that the eastern states as far west as Pennsylvania shall be included in one super-power zone; that the power shall be developed largely by steam, and that the municipal power, the railway power, and all the other power used within that zone will be switched on and off as it is required. The same thing, I am convinced, can be established in the western prairies. With a large power plant in British Columbia, one in Alberta, one in Saskatchewan and one in Manitoba-and three might be enough -sufficient power could be developed from cheap coal to operate every wheel that runs on the prairies, and at the same time to run all the municipal services in all the cities that are there now or that will be there in the future. It is by co-operation that every great achievement has been effected; and if the people of the West will co-operate, the cities with the railways and with this government, if they will take the cheap coal from the mines at Drumheller and the coal from the mines of Saskatchewan where, according to the Geological congress, there are 2,400,000,000 odd tons of coal, and establish three, if not four, super-power plants between the head of the lakes and the coast, in that way you will get an efficiency for your railways that will certainly reduce the cost of operation ultimately, if not immediately, by at least 50 per cent.
The Address-Mr. Hocken

Twelve per cent, of every ton which a locomotive draws is its own coal and water. Of every eight trains operated throughout the United States one train represents the cost of hauling the coal and water for the other seven. That should all be eliminated. We have the coal in the western provinces; we have the power of electricity, which is more efficient in the winter than in the summer. An electric locomotive never freezes up, instead of freezing it becomes more efficient the colder the weather. This plan could be put into effect one section at a time, first, say, the mountain section from Edmonton to the coast; then the section from Edmonton to Regina; then, moving east. Stop buying steam equipment and use what we have in those parts of the country not electrified, and buy instead new equipment of electric motive power until the whole of the west is put under electric power.
With transportation such as that you will be able to place the wheat of the prairies on the markets of the world at ten or fifteen cents, or perhaps more, per bushel less than at the present time. I say, as one coming from one of the central provinces, as one believing in protection for the industries, as one who knows that the industrial part of the country is bearing the load of taxation, that the resources of the eastern provinces are available to-day, for the electrification of the western railways, or the development of water transportation, to improve conditions for the western farmers and make it possible for them to earn a good livelihood.
There are bitter complaints from the prairies. Has there ever been a time when there were not bitter complaints from pioneering communities? The men on the prairies have done well; at least I have something which I might quote and which perhaps the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) will remember. It is an interview which Mr. C. W. Rowley, the western superintendent of the Bank of Commerce, had with my hon. friend, in which he points out that in less than forty years men who had gone into that country had got rich. But there was never a pioneer in Ontario who got rich in forty years.
Not rich.
He says so.
He is exaggerating.

It depends, of course,
upon what you call rich. But the men who have pioneered out there have not had anything like the difficulties, the hardships, and

the poverty which were experienced by our progenitors in this province of Ontario. It has been a comparatively easy country to the pioneer. There are, however, difficulties that are inseparable from pioneering, that is apparent. And I am satisfied that with the im-provem'ent of transportation, and if Canadians will take the thing up in a unity of spirit piece by piece, we can get a policy for the country that will be acceptable to all, a policy that will bring prosperity to all.
We in Canada have the greatest country in the world. Providence has given us a larger endowment of natural resources, and of opportunities generally, than are enjoyed by any other country. We are living in a climate that is calculated to make men strong, physically, mentally and morally. We ought to be, at the end of this century, the greatest nation in the world, able to contribute more to civilization than the Mother Country, and that is saying a great deal. There are no better people in the world than Canadians, and the climate is responsible for that. Surely, then, we ought to have the patriotism and the political capacity to get together and devise a policy which will take care of each province and promote the common interests of all. That means some 'little adjustment, some agreement; but, I am sure that" if we are all Canadians, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggests we should be, we ought to be able to do that.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to continue this debate I would like to lend my word of appreciation to the mover (Mr. Kelly) and the seconder (Mr. Lapierre) of the Address for their very able speeches. The repetition of these words of praise must be getting rather monotonous to them, but I suggest that they make the most of it; for it is possibly the last time so many kind things will be said about their speeches. To the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) I would also like to extend congratulations. They contributed very ably indeed to the discussion, and while I believe they both practically admitted that they were guilty of constituency bribery, still, we enjoyed their addresses. I think I might also very consistently extend a word of congratulation to our leader (Mr. Forke) and to the leader of the Labour group

The Address-Mr. Kellner
in the House (Mr. Woodsworth), both of whom delivered very able addresses.
I think the country can get the best outline of what a political party has to offer by watching the discussions of their adherents in their addresses during the parliamentary recess. With this in view I have read carefully the speeches of the Prime Minister during his visit in England as well as of some of the cabinet minsters who came out west this summer. Their appeal to the country on the basis of Liberal policy seemed to be that they would bring in foreign capital and immigration. There are two methods of bringing in foreign capital. One is, in some way or other, to get hold of people who have capital and bring them into the country; that method is a comparatively good one. The other would be that of adding to our national debt and also to our interest charges, and that I consider to be a very doubtful procedure indeed at this time.
At Edmonton we were favoured during the recess with two visits from the right hon. leader of the opposition. On the first occasion I went to hear him speak, and his address was a very able one. It dealt wholly, however, with a criticism of the government of the day; he dwelt at great length and very ably on the deeds of omission and commission for which the present administration was responsible. Then he returned to the East, and later he came back to the West with a man who, I think, was instrumental in again putting the province of Ontario under the domination of Toronto-and I believe it is only fair to say that in that accomplishment he strained the Conservative machine until they could not even elect Tommy Church as mayor of Toronto at the last civic election. When he arrived in Edmonton with this "Baldwin of Canada", as he was designated, another meeting was held. Unfortunately I was not able to attend, but one of those who did attend told me that on that occasion the leader of the opposition delivered a very brilliant address and again gave the government a pretty severe castigation. When he finished up he addressed his audience in words something to this effect: "It possibly would not be very fitting for me to come out here and say all these unkind things about the Liberals without saying what the Conservatives would do if they were elected. I will tell you what they would do. You have seen the farmers leave their farms in western Canada and go down across the border in great numbers. That is nothing to what has happened in Ontario; there they are leaving every city, town and village, and the country is practically deserted. What would we do? We would build a high tariff wall
around Canada and produce a home market for our farmers." There he hesitated, no doubt expecting a little applause; and I am frank to say that he is nearly always able to command it when he desires it. On that occasion, however, in that large audience, which was presumed to be a Conservative audience, there was not a clap or a "hear, hear"; not a note of appreciation could have reached his ears.
After his departure we had a third visit, from the hon. gentleman who is perhaps the heftiest member of the Conservative group in the House; I refer to the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie), who was Minister of Agriculture in the late government and who is now official organizer for the Conservative party. He came out to Edmonton, and according to the papers that are more or less loyal to that party, he was having a great deal of success in organizing the Conservatives of the district. That paper made quite a number of very favourable comments during his stay and for a day or two after he had gone, but subsequently one of the other papers came out with the rather caustic remark that since the member for Victoria had left the district it seemed that the Conservatives had all gone too; and the writer suggested that in all probability they were travelling companions of the Conservative organizer. That sort of got under the Conservatives' wool a little bit, and the Edmonton Journal came out with an article on February 11th, telling of how they had organized a smoker out there and how a number of prizes had been offered for getting members for the organization. I have the article before me; it is long and I shall not read it all, but I should like to mention some of the prizes which were offered. For the grand prize, otherwise known as the "Meighen prize", a solid gold watch. In the men's contest the first prize was the "Blair prize"-Blair, by the way, is the new provincial leader of the party in Alberta-a club bag, donated by Williaim Short; second prize, a golf bag; third prize a pocket flask; fourth prize, a gold pencil. I submit that it is a little unusual to put a gold pencil in such surroundings. The ladies also were offered some prizes. The first was a half dozen stainless steel knives with ivory handles and a half dozen 1847 Rogers dinner forks. I believe that Rogers dinner forks are manufactured in England. I submit it is rather inconsistent at least for the Conservative party to offer a prize to one of its own adherents especially at a time when the tariff is the outstanding issue, and especially a prize of knives and forks made in England.

The Address-Mr. Kellner
The second prize is a handbag, the third prize ladies' gold shoes, the fourth prize a fountain pen, and two tentative prizes are offered to the man and woman who buy over one hundred tickets. We will watch the bulletins of the member for Victoria and see how the contest goes.
I think it is a fair conclusion to draw from the information we have at the present time, that the people of Canada, those who are supporting the Liberal or the Conservative party, have the option of supporting the Liberals on the promise of foreign capital and immigration being brought in, and also on the more or less indefinite promise contained in the Speech from the Throne of a tariff reduction, or of supporting the Conservatives, who I suppose would promise them protection and an opportunity, if they lived in the province of Alberta, of winning one of these very valuable prizes. So viewing both parties and the condition that our country is in to-day, I think it is only fair to say that it is very easy to see the end of the two-party system of government in Canada. I think that possibly this parliament has a smaller number of groups than the next one will have. I do not believe the day will ever come when we will go back to the two-party system in this country again.
Neither do I attach much importance to the campaign going on in the papers of this country for a Moses to lead us out of the wilderness we are in. I believe the time has come when we shall have to take advice such as was offered us this afternoon by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), of getting together in an effort to solve the economic problem of Canada. When we do get together I hope the hon. member will not forget to send us a copy of the Orange Sentinel, because I would very much like to read its editorials when we are considering getting together in this country. However, I am fully convinced that we would be better advised to try and solve this question ourselves than to go out on a prospecting tour looking for a leader which the press tells us we need at the present time. I think that possibly that view is strengthened by the late war. Invariably after all other wars there has been some great outstanding general in the public eye, but there has been none such after this war. We had one possibly who might be termed a great organizer, but I do not think it can truthfully be said that there is one general who has come through the late war whose strategy and whose skill in battle will live in the history of our country. I

believe that point can be pressed home best perhaps by reference to an event which occurred recently in England. There they engaged a painter of considerable repute to paint three pictures, the first to be a picture of those who negotiated the Peace treaty, the second of those who signed the treaty, and the third of those who won the war. In a short time the artist completed the first picture, showing the statesmen and diplomats of the various countries negotiating the Peace treaty. Then he painted the second picture, in which he portrayed the signatories signing the treaty. But when he came to the third picture he tried one general after another in vain. According to reports he tried nine different generals and refused them all. They pressed him to hurry up and complete the series, and so finally he brought in a picture, not of any great general of the war, but of Britain's Unknown Soldier.
The Speech form the Throne conveys more or less of a promise of a reduction in the tariff. I am frank to say, after listening to the speeches which have come before the government benches, that I am more confused than ever as to what is meant by these tariff proposals. However, I am willing to be fair, and wait and see.
There are two omissions, in my opinion, in the Speech from the Throne to which I wish to call attention. I think that at the present time Canada is suffering more from the low prices which are paid to the farmer for his produce and from the excessive interest rates we have to pay than from any other two things we have to contend with. In the Speech from the Throne there may be more or less of a promise given of an attempt to reduce the cost of commodities which the farmer must buy, but I can see nothing there to give him any hope of an increase in the prices he gets for his commodities, and the interest rate is absolutely untouched.
I wish briefly to review the trade situation that Canada is in at the present time. I think it is one of the first axioms of economics that goods from one countiy must pay for goods purchased from another, and I maintain that what is largely the matter with our foreign trade at the present time is the tariff wall that we have maintained around this country, and which has kept out practically all the goods that are essential to us. About the only goods we have been able to get are the non-essentials or semi-luxuries. On the other hand, we have given to the world probably the finest wheat and the finest foodstuffs that can be grown anywhere in the civilized world to-day. The high quality of those foodstuffs is well known

The Address-Mr. Kellner
to practically every country in ithe world and to practically every individual in those countries. But the goods we are importing into this country are toys, for instance, from the Orient, silks and patent medicines from Europe -goods that might be classed as semi-luxuries. Practically no one knows the value of these goods in marketing. I believe there has grown up in our midst a merchandising combination which is taking an exorbitant toll for the service it is rendering. The United States government recently investigated this condition and found that in some cases this combination was charging as high as 1,000 per cent profit. Of course, it is pretty hard for the farmer growing wheat and Wiltshire sides to compete with profits to that extent.
We also have a few other troubles to contend with. Those of us who live in western Canada find when we come to ship our produce that the Railway Commission fixes the rates to the Great Lakes. From that point, across the Great Lakes, the rates are fixed by a combine of two men, and from there on the rates are supposed to be fixed by the competition between American and Canadian roads, but we are well informed that there is a combine between the American and Canadian roads, and that they refuse to lower the rates. Then at the ocean we have an ocean combine fixing the rates. Summing up, in shipping our goods we are up against a series of hopeless combines, and under such conditions it seems absurd to expect that a protective tariff wall is going to benefit the farmers very greatly.
There is still another policy which I have not mentioned, and that is the economic policy of doing business in Canada in such a way as to make the home market pay for the development of the foreign market. I think it is stating the case fairly to say that if a manufacturer desires to develop a foreign market, he will simply increase the price of the commodities at home, and will make the home market pay for the cost of developing that foreign market. That is the reason we often see goods manufactured in this country sold more cheaply in some foreign country than they are sold in Canada; and as a matter of fact some of our own goods, flour for example, sells more cheaply on the continent of Europe than it does here. I am convinced that in order to improve their status the farmers will have to create an organization which will be competent to handle the selling end of their business in precisely the same way. Before such an organization can be constituted, however, there is little doubt in my mind but that we shall have to get sup-13
port from other industries in Canada. We believe, speaking from the standpoint of western Canada, that the urban population very gladly extend that support at the present time. We may need some support from the government, and I am a little uneasy as to what we can expect from that quarter. Very j recently a delegation from our farmers' pool came down here and asked the acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) if he would kindly pay up a little' bill which he owed. It ! dates back to the days of the old wheat board, j when a sum of money was set aside to meet j the winding up of expenses of the board, i Those expenses were not so heavy as had 1 been expected, and besides some of the participation certificates had been destroyed. The result is that the government have about half a million dollars of our money in their custo- , dy. But when this delegation came down and asked the acting Minister of Finance if he would mind turning it over he said "No, a few years ago some of you fellows came down here and borrowed money with which to buy seed grain. You have not yet paid that money back, so I will keep this money until the other debt is paid." It is rather unfortunate he did not state that some of the people brought in under the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's immigration campaign owed for the seed grain.
I think before I leave that subject I ought to call attention to the fact that the very day the newspapers published an article about this delegation coming down to see the acting Minister of Finance, the United States papers carried a news item to the effect that a committee had been appointed there to finance the farmers of the northwestern states. I saw two reports. One said that the capital subscription was to be ten million, the other that it was to be one hundred million. I have not been able to check the statements up and I do not know which is right. But assuming that ten millions is the correct amount, it is worth while noticing the difference in attitude between the United States and Canada. In one country the government refuse to give back about half a million in their possession which actually belongs to the western farmers, in the other they are subscribing the sum of ten million dollars to assist the farmers. I think possibly such incidents as this account for a good deal of the emigration which is to-day going to the United States from this country.
Now I want to make a ferw remarks with regard to the interest rates we are paying in Canada. I think.it very fitting that I should

The Address-Mr. Kellner

remind the House that at the last session of parliament, when we were renewing the bank charters, the little group which sits in this part of the chamber asked for a number of changes in the Bank Act, changes which we hoped would probably be instrumental in reducing the interest charges and in giving us a better credit system for our country. On that occasion there was no quarrel going on about the bribing of constituencies or anything of that kind; the hand of fellowship was extended across the floor of the House by the government to the opposition at that particular time. They told us then that Canada had the finest banking system that any country ever had, and it was even suggested that we should be satisfied with it because expressions of doubt on our part might ruin our credit abroad. I think events have happened since that time which possibly show our banking system is not just as perfect as its defenders then thought it was. Quite a number of these very fine banks have got into trouble at various times. Of .ourse I am aware it will be said in each particular case "It is only a weak sister, nothing happens to the big banks ". But the big banks are strong only as long as the people have confidence in them, and when the confidence is withdrawn they are no longer able to continue. I doubt, in fact, whether a bank in any such position as that could pay its liabilities. We remember that away back in 1912, I think that was the date, one of the big banks decided to speculate in Mexican lands and the results were very disastrous. If my memory serves me correctly thirty millions were written off the books of that bank as a result of those unfortunate investments. In 1914 another bank became ambitious to enter upon railroading and had to request the assistance of the government to keep it on its feet. In 1920 another bank backed some sugar gamblers, and that bank had a sweet time to remain in business also. So I think that possibly we are entirely within our rights in discussing this financial question.
Now, I want to give the House a little idea of just how satisfactory our banking system is from a farmer's standpoint. If, say twenty years ago, a farmer wanted to buy a new binder, and his credit was good, he would go to his banker and tell him what he wished and that he desired to borrow money for the purpose. The banker would say "All right, give me your note for $150 at 8 per cent." Suppose the same farmer wanted to buy a new binder this year he would go to the banker and tell him that the old binder, having been left out in fence corners for twenty years was worn

out, and he wanted to buy a new machine. The banker would say "All right give me your note for $300 and interest for 8 per cent", or probably 9 per cent. Now the number of dollars involved is not the question at issue. The vital fact is that he wishes to perform a certain function and to get money enough to do it. In the first case he is charged $12 a year for the privilege of buying the binder, in the second case he is charged $24; and when pay day comes he discovers that the principal he has to meet in the second instance is twice the amount it was in the first.
I should like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that this is the most inopportune time the country has ever had for discussing tariff regulations, by reason of the fact that foreign exchanges are so very unstable. Practically every country outside of the United States finds that it is having a good deal of trouble in maintaining its exchange. By the way our own exchange is slipping a little within the last few days, and I doubt very much if Canada can maintain it at anywhere near the figure it is now. I think this is something the government should take under their serious consideration, as to whether they intend to permit the extra demands which were made upon the credit of our country to be met by an issue of bank credit, entailing as it does a continual payment of interest, or whether they will provide for an issue of Dominion notes to take the place of bank credit. I want to leave that subject for a moment, and I will say something further in regard to it in a few minutes.
In discussing the matter of foreign trade, I notice that the government has been particularly gratified this last few months over the fact that last year we had a favourable trade balance of about $118,000,000. Well, as I view it, possibly that is not a matter of very great gratification at all. I think it amounts to about this, that extra money could do one of three different things. It could pay the interest on our foreign debt, if we made arrangements for that in our budget. It could go back to the country as a hidden asset, or in some way that would deceive the people. It chiefly comes by increasing our national debt, and also by increasing our interest obligation. I maintain that if we are going out to try to capture foreign markets by competition, by the cheapness with which we can sell our goods to other countries, regardless of whether or not we are prepared to take their goods in payment, then we are adopting practically the policy that used to be in vogue in the military ages. There was a time in the history of the world when the country which could go

The Address-Mr. Kellner
forth and by force of its arms conquer new territory was the most prosperous and the most-to-be-envied country of all. That condition is changed to-day, and we are endeavouring to accomplish the same thing through the trade of Canada, but I believe that one method is as much as the other, merely wading through slaughter to a throne.
We have heard a great deal in this House since the debate started about the unity of eastern and western Canada, and I submit there is only one way that that can be maintained. There must be an economic advantage to all the various sections of Canada in the union or eventually it is going to dissolve. I am sure there is no one at the present time who is desirous of seeing such a dissolution, but when the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hoclcen) this afternoon pointed out the horrible plight Brantford was getting into, and told us it was our duty to maintain the tariff, so as to hold up Brantford and some of these other cities, I could not help but think that these cities would never have been there if it had not been for the tariff: and having built these towns and brought them to their present state of development, if we find they are too heavy to carry, I am afraid we will have to get out from under the load, regardless of whether it means a dissolution of the union or not.
I would like to make a few remarks about the unsympathetic way in which the demands of the West have been met by eastern Canada and by this parliament in particular, and possibly I could cite nothing that would bring the matter home more truly than the question of the natural resources. We have been demanding the natural resources; and, for that matter, have been promised them by every parliament which we have ever had in Canada, regardless of its political affiliations. I remember when this government was elected they were trying to find a seat for the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) in the province of Alberta. I asked one of their agents why they wanted him down in Ottawa so particularly. "Well" he said, "If there is a man in western Canada who can get the natural resources for us, that man is Charlie Stewart." He came down in 1921, this is 1924 and we have not got the natural resources yet.
Then there is the matter of the Branch Lines bill. That bill went through this House last year without any very serious opposition. It was defeated in another section of parliament, the mention of which is taboo at the present time; but I would like to suggest to the government that there might be a 13i
possibility this year of getting that bill through, if they would change their methods of financing a little. We have had two or three instances in the past of the adoption of different methods. Back in 1916 the government came to the aid of the Canadian Northern Railway with a grant of sixteen million dollars, and they came to the aid of ' the Grand Trunk Pacific with a grant of ten million dollars. That money was simply turned over to those railway companies in exchange for securities, and went into circulation, to meet construction costs and operating costs of the road. I can see no reason at this present time, having in mind the situation of our finances to-day why the government should not make an issue of Dominion notes to pay for these branch line railways. It would save the interest bill which is bound to accrue if we finance it in. the ordinary channels, and I think that the only objection that could be raised to the suggestion is that increasing the amount of the circulation without increasing production, *would cause prices to go up. I think that objection would fall flat, because if that money were expended in this way, we would very materially increase production. During last session the members in this part of the House were quite frequently referred to as the calamity howlers of parliament. I think it is only fair to say that this year the calamity howlers have largely changed their positions. ]Mr. Harris.]
find that our increases in exports are in commodities which require the services in this country of hewers of wood and drawers of water. The heads of this institution, one of these manufacturing institutions some hon. gentlemen are wont to call parasites, sleep in a room at night with a telephone beside their bed and are ready to do business whenever it rings. All their long-distance business is done at night, to save time during the day and, incidentally, because they get a little cheaper rate. They have worked four-
teen hours a day for thirty-eight or forty years and have built up in that time a business worth $452,000. Perhaps they are parasites; perhaps not; in my humble opinion they are not. In 1020 they took a loss, without any depreciation or interest of $92,600; in 1921 tjjey took a loss of $37,800; in 1922 they took a loss of $12,731. Interest and depreciation charges in that time amounted to $100,000, so the work of these two stalwart men, with their nineteen children, over a period of forty years was wiped out of existence. I am not crying hard times in this House, but I uphold the men, who after an experience of that kind were found-where0 They were found in their place of business at eight o'clock on Saturday morning with their sons in overalls and the head of the institution in a smock going around and doing the best they could-for what? For the future of this country and their children.
_ Mr. Speaker, when I hear hon. members in this House rise in their place and say that the people in the large centres are parasites and things of that kind, it makes my blood boil. I heard the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) the other evening say something about the party in this comer of the House. What he said about the egg that was only a nest egg, and only a rock at that, rather amused me. I noticed after he had got through that the bird had not even laid an egg. What we want more than anything else in this country is to get on common ground with one another. We in Ontario love, admire^ and respect, the people in the western provinces. I represent several thousand people in the county of York. I live on the farm myself during the summer months, in a four roomed house and I know something about farming conditions. I have raised as many as eight and nine hundred hogs at one season.
I know what it is to grow five thousand bags of potatoes in a year. In my boyhood I have known what it was to hoe potatoes from early morning till late at night. Mr. Speaker, if you go back twenty years and look up the population in the county of York you will find as many of our sons and daughters have gone to the western provinces as are left to look after the interest of our fair county. Thinking of the remark that fell from the lips of the hon. member for Nelson the other evening that he wanted to see the traditions in the back of the heads of the people who came to that country, I can scarcely understand the views that are being enunciated here by that hon. member. I know that the brothers and sisters, sons and daughters, and

The Address-Mr. Harris
relatives of the people who left the county of York to go west have not in their makeup such sentiments as have been expressed from the left hand corner of this House.
When the sarcastic laughter came from my good friends to the left I was talking about the exodus of some of the people from our country, and I was saying how sad and sorrowful we felt to see these young people quitting Canada. If hon. members will devote a thought to the city of Toronto and to the number of homes there they will see how important this question of employment is. It will be seen that there are quite a number of people engaged in the building trades there, while a number find employment in the province at large. There are some 25,500 heads of families engaged in the building trades in the province of Ontario and last year they drew in wages $28,470,174.
These people have another grievance which I want to explain as briefly as possible. That grievance is against the sales tax. Now, you may wonder how it is that working men have a grievance against that tax. My reason for mentioning the matter at this time is to afford the government an opportunity of reviewing the situation and providing relief before the budget is brought down. According to the act,-taking into consideration the work of stonemasons, sheet metal workers, and builders,-all work done at the job on any particular building is exempt from sales tax; but work wrought in stone or any sheet metal moulded into shape within a factory or shop is liable to the sales tax of 6 per cent. Now, Mr. Speaker, in a large centre of population like Toronto the municipal, provincial and federal institutions, and the citizens generally, are all urged to do as much work as possible during the winter months. Unfortunately, industries of the kind that I have described find that when they do this work in their plants they have to pay the sales tax of 6 per cent. Consequently, in order to avoid that tax they endeavour to have the work wrought as much as possible on the job. The result is that they will hold back building that necessitates that class of work until the weather permits them to get on the job. Representations have been made to the government for a change in the law such as would meet the conditions of these workers but up to the present time no relief has been afforded. I think I will read to the House, if hon. members will bear with me for a moment a few lines from a letter which one of these large contractors has sent to me on the subject:
I might say that we have at present a large contract on Trinity College, Toronto, and through some
persuasion we induced the architect, with an object in view of keeping our men employed, to have certain woodwork delivered at our factory to be covered with sheet metal. This woodwork could be covered on the building and would come under the heading of erection or installation, but we discovered that by doing this in our factory we were subject to a sales tax of 6 per cent on the labour only, and we made inquiries through the Customs department, and their ruling was that we had the option of doing the work at the building and avoiding the sales tax or doing it at our factory and paying sales tax. In other words, they did not consider the men being out of employment, their business was to collect the sales tax.
Mr. Speaker, conditions in Toronto between contractors and their employees are very amiable. They work together for the good of the citizens to the very best of their ability with the happiest results. I have also a letter from the international representative of the Sheet Metal Workers on the same subject addressed to the Hon. James Murdock, Minister of Labour, Ottawa, Ontario. I think the minister is going to follow me, and I hope he will take a note of this matter. Perhaps he will promise us to-night that some relief will be granted. The extract I wish to read is as follows:
It has been the policy of our employers in past years to try to get enough contracts ahead, that would keep their regular employees busy during the winter months, by making this work from detail drawings for construction jobs.
If this sales tax is continued on labour in our trade, the results will be, that our employers will stop making this work in the shops and will avoid paying this extra 6 per cent tax on labour, by waiting till the buildings are well under construction, and have all our work manufactured on the job, the results of this will be detrimental to our members, placing 60 per cent of our membership on the unemployment list, for the winter months, and in our opinion will only slightly increase the revenue to the Department of Finance.
While this will affect our trade greatly, on building construction work, it also affects a number of other building trades unions to a large extent, and I feel assured that in the interest of labour you will take this matter up at your earliest convenience, to the end that this coming session of parliament will amend the act, to apply on material only, so that our members, and many others will not be added to the unemployment list during the winter months of 1924-25.
They received a reply from the Minister of Customs and Excise and also the Minister of Labour. In that reply, according to the document I have in my possession, both ministers evaded the question at issue entirely, and merely quoted for the benefit of the contractors and their employees a part of the act.
Will my hon. friend read the reply from the Customs department?

I have already written for that reply, I have not got it here. If the minister would like me to read another letter from the international representatives of some

We know there are some Tories amongst them.

I was -talking about some of the things that are affecting the citizens of Toronto. One of them is the necessity for better custom house accommodation. The first minister is not present to-night, and no one knows which minister is acting for the Post Office Department. But let me point this out: The city of Toronto yields a greater postal revenue to the Dominion exchequer than the city of Montreal and all the rest of the cities in the province of Quebec combined.
