They speak of this government studying economy and retrenchment, something which I very strongly advocated myself last session and again advocate just now. I ask this government to look into the matter of postal service in our large centres, and endeavour to get back to the pre-war rate for drop-letters, not only in Toronto but in the whole of the Dominion.
I am satisfied that the increased volume of business which they would receive would in

part compensate any loss the government might sustain in this direction.
I have told hon. members once or twice to-night that I am supposed to do my best to represent 110,000 of the finest people in the Dominion of Canada. I notice in the Speech from the Throne that a redistribution bill will be brought down. I also remember very well that the first minister of the Crown promised this House that that measure would be equitable. I earnestly trust that he is sincere in that, and I sincerely hope the government will give the home-loving people of the constituency I represent adequate representation in this House. I am satisfied to represent 110,000 people in this House, if everyone else will do the same-anything to cut down the overhead in running this country. We can carry on with one hundred men and women in this House, if we will. I would do anything to cut down the excess county councils, city councils and all sorts of municipal bodies which exist at the present time. We have too much legislation. It is costing us too much. Take West York.

I am quite open to anything the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) will suggest. I am sure the first minister of the Crown when he makes his appeal to some 30,000 people-I do not say that he will be successful at the next election-will not be addressing an audience which is any more intelligent than an audience in East York, representative of 110,000 people. I trust this government will see to it that we have a just and equitable redistribution, so that all kinds and classes of citizens will have more or less equal representation in this House.
Louder.

The hon. gentleman says "louder." I was just speaking about the first minister of the Crown. Some years ago I was in a little village called Bolton in North York. The first minister of the Crown -and I am sorry he is not here to-night- was telling the populace about the great principles of the Liberal party. An old gentleman in the back of the hall rose and said

The Address-Mr. Harris
"louder." No attention was paid to him and a few moments later he again called out "louder." In the middle of the hall was another man who was much older than the man in the rear of the hall, and who knew something about politics and other things in the Dominion of Canada; he rose and said to the gentleman who was calling "louder," "It is all right my friend, sit down and rest yourself. I am absolutely sincere in what I have said to this House, and I believe that everything I have said up to this moment is absolutely true, and it is in the minds and hearts of the people of Canada. If my hon. friend does not think so, I will pass the hat around this assembly and gather enough money to buy a box of cigars; I will place him on a railway train, let him sit in the smoking car, travel from Halifax to Vancouver, and listen to what he hears from the public-and what he will hear on the trains in Canada is from the lips of salesmen, business men, people who are wont to travel, people who in the first essential are optimistic, because otherwise they would not hold down the positions they occupy-and if he can come back to this House and say to us, that the conditions under which the Dominion is operating at the present time, due to the policy of this government in part, are what they should be, or if he can say that 40 per cent, or less than half, of the people he meets are satisfied with the government that is functioning here and now from the treasury benches, then I will give him my seat in this House.
Last session, Mr. Speaker, I suggested to the House that in the interests of the people of Canada we should have a free, frank, open discussion, so that the people could get some idea as to the magnitude and the necessity of the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway, in order that they could express themselves as to the necessity or non-necessity of the work. I was criticized by the hon. Minister of Finance in his budget speech for making that suggestion. I welcome criticism. I did not like to interrupt the minister because I sympathized with his predicament at that time. I realized the strain he was under due to the many duties he had to perform. But let me answer the minister now. I am sorry to have to do it in his absence. The words and sentiments which I expressed last session are now coming to life. The government have faced both ways on this question and now they are facing our way. The Montreal influence must have slackened or been diverted in some way or another;
and the government came forward with the announcement that they have made representations to Washington and I trust it will not end up with correspondence only, but that they will put before the people of the country the necessity of this project being put through to a conclusion.
Some of us who do not know a great deal, perhaps, about matters political have been wondering why it is necessary for the first minister of the Crown and one-half of his cabinet each year to go abroad and attend all kinds of conferences, Imperial, economic and labour. I suppose the necessity is there; but with only a population of nine million, with this country scattered as it is, with the differences of opinion and the necessity for all getting together upon common ground and trying to get a definite policy which will be more satisfactory than the present one, in my humble opinion it is time the people of Canada demanded of the ministers a little more of their time at home, a little less travelling abroad, a few more conferences within the Dominion itself, not a hurried conference with Premier Dunning and the member for Marquette, (Mr. Crerar) taking place perhaps in a day or two days, not a case of bargaining or something of that nature, but let us have a big, open conference, let us put all our troubles into the pot, and see if we cannot bring forth a policy which will be more satisfactory than the policy we have at the present time. I like to feel that (I can advocate something which not only bears on my own constituency, but something which will work for the general good of the people of the Dominion.
Last year I said something with reference to the province and city of Quebec. I ask you to think of that line of railway which we have lying on our backs, that Grand Trunk Pacific, running across the northern part of that province. I advocated very strongly that our western friends urge the government to do everything possible to have the freight rates from Winnipeg to Quebec city lowered and to have better port facilities provided for Quebec city so that our western friends would have lower carrying charge and better facilities for getting their products to the markets of the world. Some notice was taken of that. I notice that 5,000 cattle were shipped from Quebec to the old country last year. I hope the number will be 15,000 this year.
Hear, hear.

I was correcting a quotation.	.

Emerson says:
Any body politic or otherwise that is wont to follow a policy and follow that policy beyond the realm of the good of the people in any body or any country will find that that policy will turn to carrion, and that carrion will be a stench in the nostrils of the people of that community.
I say to the hon. member for East Lamb-ton (Mr. Fansher), who is wont to talk about the eagles and carrion, that in the province of Ontario on June 25 last we had an example of what happened when Drury carried their policy so far in Ontario that it became carrion and a stench in the nostrils of the people of that province, with the result that on June 25 his party were put in then-place and another party was put in charge.
I do not like those expressions. We are all one people in this country. We in the cities are no better than you people in the country. We realize that you are good citizens, but we feel that we are as good citizens as you are. We want to get on common ground with you. We want you to intermingle with us and to help us out in our difficulties, and we in turn will help you out in yours.
In that connection I have much pleasure in supporting the amendment moved to the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I support it whole heartedly because I know there are coming into this country at the present time a large number of commodities which can be grown on the farms of Ontario, the good province of Quebec and the provinces of the West. The grain imports last year amounted to $11,100,000; vegetables, $4,800,000; without any rubber. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) will be worrying about the rubber, but there, is no rubber in these imports. Fruits amounted to, $26,000,000; nuts, $3,600,000. This makes a

total of $45,500,000. If this government feels disposed to impose a tariff against them to raise revenue and incidentally to keep them out of the country, and if the government feels disposed to make us eat rhubarb by keeping bananas out of the country, I say more power to them and I will support them. In this way they will be raising a revenue by keeping these commodities out of the country and incidentally giving more markets for the products which the people who live on the farms are able to produce.
A policy which will help our large centres of population in this matter must be the policy in vogue in this Dominion, if we are going to keep step with the other nations of the world. It is hinted in the Speech from the Throne that the government is going to do something drastic with an industry that has been established here for some time, the agricultural implement industry. Does this government honestly believe that it is doing the people of Canada any service by intimating to this one industry that it is to be the goat for bargaining for the support of our friends to my left? Do my hon. friends opposite not know enough about the agricultural implement business to know that they are only driving the few scattered businesses that are at present working in Canada together into one great combine probably centred in Chicago? In the final analysis, are you not going to pay just as much for those implements if you drive the industry into the hands of one concern? I know some hon. members will be thinking of watered stock and all that sort of thing. There are about 110,000 people in my riding. Upon an analysis of the businesses in that particular riding I find that there is not one which has any watered stock. This talk about watered stock is all humbug. There may be an isolated case of watered stock, but as a general rule there is very 'little in the business of this country. Furthermore, so far as my own riding is concerned, I do not know of one man who is worth five hundred thousand dollars; nor can I recall more than two or three who are worth more than a hundred thousand dollars. There are more men in this group beside me worth more than a hundred thousand dollars than there are in my riding. Now, these industries are employing a number of very good citizens; they are employing some of our sons and daughters who are a better type of citizens than you could bring into the country by any system of immigration that you may have at the back of your minds. Certainly they are better than the people you could get by the scheme partly enunciated by my hon. friend from
Prince Edward Island (Mr. Sinclair). These people desire to stay in Canada; but if this government persists in the policy which they have enunciated-as a matter of fact they have not enunciated any policy; they have merely hinted that they are apt to do something in this direction-then I sincerely believe that they will do untold damage to the prospects of this Dominion. I am sincere; I am as sincere as is the hon. member for Nelson. I am sorry in a way that he was so sincere, because I could not agree with his views. But I am satisfied that if the government follow the policy which they hint at they will upset the industrial fabric of this country to an incalculable extent.
As I said at the outest, Mr. Speaker, I did not intend taking part in this discussion; I have merely been filling in, so to speak. There are half a dozen things which I should like to touch upon but I shall have to leave them until a later day in the session. However, let me close for the present with one statement which I think is of general interest to the country. We are ready and are very anxious to get on common ground with the difficulties that our people in the western provinces have, and we ask in behalf of the people in the large centres of population that those of the West shall try to get on common ground with us and help to bring this Dominion to the position which she should hold within this Empire.

I desire to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address on the speeches which they have delivered in this debate. With regard to the Speech from the Throne, there are I think a number of paragraphs which would indicate that the government intend to go at least some distance in the direction in which I myself and some other members in this House would like to see them go. And from the speeches that have come from hon. members to my right it would seem that they expect that the government will travel some way in that direction. Without committing myself to any approval of the Speech in all its details, I will simply say at the moment that we will wait and see what the results will be when the budget comes down. So far as the legislation that will be introduced to the House is concerned, the general tone of the Speech indicates that the government is willing to go a part of the way with us and to give us at least some of the things for which we have been asking for a number of years. I do not know whether this will be considered as bargaining for support or not; I do not know

The Address-Mr. Kennedy (Edmonton)
whether hon. members to my right will describe it as dishonourable bargaining. But if the government comes down with legislation which I believe to be in the interests of the country, legislation which we have been asking for, then of course it will simply put us in the position that will compel us to support them. We have before us an amendment which is somewhat vague. There is an expression of regret with regard to present conditions in agriculture. There is the statement that the Speech from the Throne-
While embodying a distinct threat to an important section of industry, contains no promise of legislation which will tend to retain and enlarge the home market for our own Canadian producers.
That Suggests that the mover of the amendment would still further protect our manufacturing industries and in that way give us a larger home market. We have been following that policy in this country for a good many years. It was in 1878 that there was introduced in Canada the National Policy which was going to make this country independent of foreign countries and give our farmers a home market that would make them completely independent of the rest of the world. I have taken the trouble during the last few days to compile some figures with regard to what this National Policy has cost Canada. When criticising the budget of 1921, on May 10th, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), speaking about the reductions that had been made in the Liberal tariff, after the Liberals had come into power in 1896, made the following statement, as may be seen by reference to page 3151 of Hansard of the year I have stated:
But it must be remembered-and economists, I think, will agree-that the saving you make in a case like that is not to be measured only by the amount that you did not pay into the Customs; you have to take into account also the check that was put upon the rise of prices at home, and that for every dollar saved to the people in that direct way probably two dollars were saved in the difference between the prices prevailing and those which would otherwise have been charged by the home manufacturer.
Taking that as a basis on which to compute what this National Policy has cost us, I find that the total revenue collected as a result of the tariff from 1879 to 1922 amounted to the large sum of 12,310,417,676. If assistance has been given to the manufacturing industries of Canada to twice the extent of the customs collections, it would seem that they have received assistance to a total of four billions.
I suppose there are some who will object to that on the ground that in some cases farm

produce is protected. However, I will try to show later on that the customs tariff, so far as the farming industry is concerned, is absolutely useless as a means of keeping up prices. In any case, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, and taken in conjunction with the total amount of customs revenue collected in Canada from 1879 to 1922, the National Policy has cost this country four billions of dollars. I cannot help thinking of that fact when I hear hon. members talking about the sales tax and the income tax. Whatever objections there may be to the sales tax and to the income tax, I do not think it means such a tremendous additional cost to the people over and above the actual amount that goes into the treasury as is involved in the tariff. We have heard a good deal of argument with regard to objections raised by people of the West against the continuance of this protective policy. The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Harris) said that hon. members on his side were willing to take the matter up with us and find out if we could not get on common ground. Well it is going to be an exceedingly difficult matter for us to get on common ground if we pay and they collect; if we have to pay this protection while industries centred in Toronto and other industrial communities throughout the Dominion get the advantage. I do not see where there is any equity in that, nor am I convinced that the government can provide for taxation for industrial organizations in any other way. We do not produce any revenue here; we do not create any wealth, and when we follow a policy of this kind we are merely taking money out of the pockets of the people who are unprotected and putting it into the pockets of the people who are protected.
I find that though we have given this tremendous assistance, especially to the manufacturing industries, the total invested capital of those industries in Canada, according to the Canada Year Book of 1921, is just a little over three billion dollars. So it would seem that we have actually, through the operation of the customs tariff, provided them with sufficient to pay the whole invested capital in those industries throughout the Dominion. We have about three billions in manufacturing industries, about two billions in railways and about three billions in the value of farm property. Whatever benefits may have come to any part of Canada from such a policy as this have cost the rest of Canada more than they are worth. You can pay too much for anything, no matter what it is, and I think in this regard we have paid too

The Address-Mr. Kennedy (Edmonton)
much for the protected industries of this country. The result has been that manufacturing has got far ahead of what it ought to be. I have before me an article by C. Howard Smith, President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, published in the Canadian Congress Journal for February, 1924. It says:
Our taxes at present are staggering. Why? Chiefly because of the smallness of our population. Our overhead is too great. We have enough machinery now in Dominion, provincial and municipal governments to govern fifty millions of people, instead of nine. We have enough railways to serve two or three times our population. Our present system of manufacturing, banking, retailing and wholesaling could provide for the wants of many additional millions, with very little additional expense. Our taxes are only high in proportion to our population.
If the manufacturing industries of Canada can only exist behind a large protective tariff, what is the use of having them developed far ahead of the needs of the country? In the very nature of things that result is undesirable. The surplus, if there is any so far as manufactured goods are concerned, has got to go out of the country to compete in outside markets, in countries which in many cases have depreciated currencies, countries which, the manufacturers claim, have large advantages when it comes to manufacturing articles that are similar to those produced in Canada. If they can compete outside of Canada, why not inside? If they cannot compete outside, then they have got to restrict their output to the needs of Canada, and there should not exist a tariff which develops industry far in advance of the needs of the country.
When our farmers were flooding into the West, when there was plenty of free land, the situation was different so far as the agricultural implement industry was concerned. I had some relations with one of the large machinery establishments in the West and I remember the time when a man on the frontier at the end of the railway, selling agricultural machinery to a large homestead area, would sell a tremendous amount; it was stated that one agent sold a quarter pf a million dollars' worth in one year. In those boom days, with protective tariffs, and with a large market owing to the settlement of western Canada, the manufacturers went on and made money. Thinking that it was a permanent thing in Canada, I suppose, they developed their industry far in exess of the needs of the country as they stand to-day, and the result is that they are having hard times. We have possibly too many industries; we certainly have too many if they cannot compete outside of Canada. So we are being bombarded to-day with requests for 14

If with all the assistance which has been given by the Dominion to- these manufacturing industries, and particularly by the people who are unprotected, they are unable to stand on their own feet, then I want to say that the policy has miserably failed and the sooner we get away from it the better.
Owing to the financial strength which these industries have attained due to the generous policy pursued by the Dominion, they have been able to hire brains; they have built up splendid marketing organizations, and in a great many cases there has been established complete monopoly of the sale and distribution of the products, which is another thing that enables -them to take full advantage of the protective tariff. When anybody says that we can protect agriculture as we have protected industries, I say that we cannot do it. It might be possible, if we got wheat pools in western Canada, or one wheat pool that would control the output of the western farmer, to take advantage of a protective tariff, but we cannot do it as long as we are selling individually as we have been doing. There was a time when we had a monopoly organization marketing Canadian wheat-the Wheat Board of 1919; and the government of that day understood this principle very thoroughly. I have before me Order in Council No. 1589, dated at the Government House, Ottawa, Thursday, the 31st day of July, 1919. It says:
The board shall have power from time to time:
(a) To take delivery of wheat in Canada at any point.
(c) To sell wheat so delivered to millers in Canada for milling purposes at such prices and subject to such conditions as the board sees fit, the price of sale to millers being governed as nearly as may be by the price obtainable at the same time in the world's markets for wheat of equal value, regard being had to the cost of transport, handling and storage.
That is a provision, I take it, to prevent the board from taking advantage of the Canadian consumers at that time.

There is a reference in the Speech from the Throne to the question of branch railways. I myself am interested in a particular branch railway. I have the good fortune or the misfortune, to represent a constituency that comprises almost one-half the area of the province of Alberta. The railway system that serves that constituency centres in Edmonton and there are three railways, one running to the west, one to the northwest and one to the north. Though in a geographical sense we are tributary to the western coast, to Vancouver and Prince Rupert, owing to the railway system we have developed in the Dominion of Canada we are made tributary to Fort William and Montreal.
I am very anxious to get a railway built that will put a base on the triangle connecting up those three railways running in a westerly and northerly direction from Edmonton-that will connect the Canadian National railway running west to Whitecourt, the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia to Grand Prairie, and other points in the Peace River district to the Canadian National railway somewhere east of the mountains. I may say that this has been a dream of the people who are living north and west of the city of Edmonton ever since they settled that country, and unless we get that railway within some time in the near future the result will be disastrous so far as the settlers are con-

cemed. I think the cry "If we do not get just what we want when we want it we will leave the country" has been overdone. Nevertheless, I have this to say: Although last year we had one of the best crops in the history of the country there are a large number of people leaving the district. We have heard a great deal about economy in the form of articles and periodicals during the last few months, and the po.int has been stressed in speeches delivered in the present debate. Economy may be all right if it is correctly interpreted. I believe the expenditure I am urging would be in the interest of true economy. No doubt a great many will say the same thing with regard to their particular requests to the government, but if it is not true economy to bring a large section of Canada, one of the richest producing sections of it, to the seaboard eight hundred miles away, and keep it tributory to the seaboard three thousand miles distant-I think that is about the mileage-then I do not know what economy means. We are dealing with a transportation system, in so far as our settlers are concerned, that is very costly and in order to save the settlers there we want to get the very best railway service that is possible in view of the geographical situation of the district and its resources. It may be said that we cannot afford this expenditure at the present time, but I want to point out that we have in that district the very products that have been furnishing a large tonnage for the railways of Canada. From Edmonton westward to the coast, formerly the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern were in competition but they have been consolidated into one system west of Edmonton to Redpath Junction. To a point 150 miles west of Edmonton the territory is revenue producing, but from there to the coast there is not a large revenue producing territory at the present time. The statement has been made from time to time that in order to make the National Railways pay they must obtain tonnage. Very well, in the territory of which I speak there is a splendid opportunity to 14i
obtain tonnage. We have coal, timber and wheat in that area in abundance, and there is the possibility of producing wheat in tremendous quantities. I have here comparisons of the quantities of the total railway freight carried for October, 1923, and October, 1922, on the railways of Canada. I find that the total amounts of products hauled by all the railways, and loaded at Canadian stations, were:-Agricultural 15,751,874 tons; products of the mine 12,353,153 tons; products of the forest 8,695,722 tons; manufactures and miscellaneous, 11,636,183 tons. According to the statement of October, 1923 of the total of 4,205,335 tons of agricultural products, 3,142,953 tons represent wheat; bituminous coal is represented to the' extent of 1,006,442 tons out of a total of 1,969,922 tons loaded. When we come to forest products we find there is also a very large percentage of the total loaded in that division Here is a chance for the Minister of Railways to construct a branch that is at present productive and will be for all time to come, that is not a duplication of another system, and that will go a long way towards helping to solve the problem resulting from the lack of business so far as our National Railways are concerned.
I want to say that I am particularly interested and pleased with the showing the National Railways have made during the last few years, and the steady improvement that we have seen so far as those railways are concerned but I think there is a good deal of unjust criticism with regard to the system We find, for instance, there is a duplication west of Edmonton. There are few hundred miles of track there of very costly construction that are absolutely worthless and yet interest must be paid on the bonds. We find that the Canadian Pacific Railway, with all its branch lines in western Canada, after having been established for a number of years has only one line of railway through the barren country north of lake Superior, whereas the National Railways is under the disadvantage of maintaining and helping to pay interest on two railway systems in that region. So that if we have deficits we may attribute them in part to the fact that we have two systems instead of one to maintain. Yet, in spite of that, very satisfactory progress is being made on our National Railways and the showing has improved greatly during the last few years.

We have heard a great deal about the question of secession. I may say there are a great many people in western Canada talking about it to-day, and they are not foreigners. I am not anxious to see the West pull away from the East, but I desire to say that confederation can only be justified when it is in the best interests of all the people of Canada. It is not justified as an end in itself. It is only justified as the best means to serve all people in this Dominion. While the Speech from the Throne expresses the desire for corrective legislation that will lead to unity in the Dominion, I say that we can never have real, satisfactory lasting union until we can convince all our people that they are getting the same kind of treatment in the Maritime provinces and in the prairies as they are getting in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, or vice versa.
If we are going to have all of the disadvantages and none of the advantages of the tariff, and if our freight rates are going to be possibly, fifteen, twenty or maybe twenty-five per cent higher than they are in some other parts of Canada, and if, in addition to that, we have a bank interest rate that runs about two per cent higher than in some of the more thickly settled districts of the Dominion, I do not know how to convince any intelligent person that the treatment of all parts is equitable. The people in the West are very vigorous in their demands. I am not referring merely to the members. I am glad we have a people that are not satisfied with those conditions and will never be satisfied until they are rectified. I believe that until they get freight rates that are just about the same from coast to coast we never will have anything like real satisfaction or real unity between the various provinces of the Dominion of Canada.
